title: Does Your Neural Network Extrapolate? Feature Engineering as Identifiability Bias for OOD Generalization

paper.title: Does Your Neural Network Extrapolate? Feature Engineering as Identifiability Bias for OOD Generalization
paper.abstract:
Abstract Successful deep neural networks discover salient features of data.
We show when and why they fail to learn out-of-distribution (OOD)-relevant representations from an in-distribution (ID) training window.
This requires decoupling feature learning from data-generating-process (DGP) identifiability.
From a single training window, OOD extrapolation is non-identifiable: infinitely many DGPs are ε \varepsilon -observationally equivalent on the training data but diverge arbitrarily outside it, and no in-distribution criterion alone reliably breaks the tie.
A structural commitment, the feature map, label map, and model class ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) , dictates the assumed DGP and governs OOD generalization while leaving ID performance essentially unchanged.
When architecture, pretraining, augmentation, input formats, or domain knowledge implicitly inject the missing commitment, the model succeeds.
When it cannot infer OOD-relevant structure from ID evidence, it fails.
Changing only the representation can make the same architecture, at the same in-distribution loss, differ by ∼ 520 × {\sim}520\times out of distribution.
When the commitment is correct and identifiable, OOD error vanishes.
For example, Fourier coordinates turn periodic extrapolation into interpolation on 𝕊 1 \mathbb{S}^{1} .
The same mechanism predicts outcomes in three natural-science settings (mass-action chemistry; Kepler’s-third-law exoplanet prediction, n = 2,362 n=2{,}362 ; and cross-species coding-DNA detection) and in a 264-run positional-encoding study across Transformer, Mamba, and S4D.
Finally, a controlled study shows: correct features are necessary but not sufficient.
The model class must express the target, and the transformed training data must cover the relevant representation space.
Thus, feature engineering is not a departure from what makes deep learning successful.
It is the explicit structural commitment that makes extrapolation identifiable.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Left: sin ⁡ ( x ) \sin(x) (green) and its degree-9 Taylor polynomial (black) can be observationally equivalent (depending on noise and amount of samples) on the training window and diverge on [ π , 3 ​ π ] [\pi,3\pi] . Models (MLP, SINDy, TabPFN, TimesFM) trained/evaluated on the Original (raw) space without noise are shown. Right: in Fourier coordinates φ ⁡ ( x ) = ( sin ⁡ x , cos ⁡ x ) \varphi(x)=(\sin x,\cos x) , both (ID, OOD) map to the same circle 𝕊 1 \mathbb{S}^{1} , turning OOD extrapolation into interpolation. While the Universal Approximation Theorem guarantees that neural networks are exceptional interpolators within the support of their training data, they struggle with out-of-distribution extrapolation. Frameworks from Statistical Learning Theory provide guarantees for in-distribution generalization, however, achieving mathematically guaranteed extrapolation in deep learning remains an unsolved problem. We believe it is the right time to ask the question: When can neural networks extrapolate? We start our journey with a good old sin ⁡ ( x ) \sin(x) function. A neural network, 5 5 -hidden-layer MLP with 256 256 Tanh units, trained on raw f ⁡ ( x ) = sin ⁡ ( x ) f(x)=\sin(x) on [ − π , π ] [-\pi,\pi] ( Fig. 1 ) extrapolates as a smooth, eventually-levelling curve with high OOD relative error while an identical architecture trained on φ ⁡ ( x ) = ( sin ⁡ x , cos ⁡ x ) \varphi(x)=(\sin x,\cos x) reaches OOD relative error below 1 % 1\% ( Tab. 1 ). The two have indistinguishable training loss; they differ only in the feature map applied before the model. Two assumptions, periodic and polynomial-like (Taylor is a valid hypothesis on [ − π , π ] [-\pi,\pi] ), can be observationally equivalent on the training window and diverge outside it. The indistinguishability problem is structural. For any finite training window W W , infinitely many processes agree on W W to any fixed tolerance and disagree arbitrarily outside it. Proposition 1 formalises this as a worst-case lower bound on any in-distribution test, and cross-validation (CV) falls short empirically even outside that worst case ( Sec. 6.1 ). The modeller’s choice of representation space and model class breaks the tie. Correctness is relative to the model class. ( sin ⁡ x , cos ⁡ x ) (\sin x,\cos x) is the correct φ \varphi for sin ⁡ ( x ) \sin(x) only because the downstream class favours linear combinations: it renders the target linearly expressible. A Fourier-series regressor would collapse φ \varphi to the identity. Correctness is a joint property of ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) , which is why we treat them as a single commitment ( Sec. 3 ). Concrete failures of correct φ \varphi paired with non-matching ℳ \mathcal{M} appear in Sec. 4 . Three conditions are jointly necessary: (a) a representation ( φ , ψ ) (\varphi,\psi) aligned with the DGP, (b) a model class that expresses the target between 𝒵 x \mathcal{Z}_{x} and 𝒵 y \mathcal{Z}_{y} , and (c) coverage of 𝒵 x \mathcal{Z}_{x} sufficient to identify the model. (a)+(b) constitute the DGP commitment; (c) is its evidential prerequisite ( Sec. 7 ). The headline comparisons hold (b) and (c) fixed, isolating (a). Contributions: (i) We formalise observational equivalence on a finite window, identify ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) as the DGP commitment, prove ERM on W W is structurally blind to the choice, and characterise near-boundary data of width δ ≥ ε / r \delta\geq\varepsilon/r as the minimum heuristic that breaks the blindness ( Sec. 3 ). (ii) We isolate φ \varphi , ψ \psi , and ℳ \mathcal{M} in controlled experiments ( Sec. 4 ) on minimal pairs and on pretrained foundation models (TimesFM ( Das et al., 2024 ) , TabPFN ( Hollmann et al., 2025 ) , governed by the same mechanism via input format). (iii) We validate cross-domain ( Sec. 5 ) on chemistry (mass-action kinetics), physics (Kepler exoplanets, n = 2,362 n{=}2{,}362 ), and biology (cross-species coding-DNA-sequence (CDS) detection on six organisms), same prediction, all confirmed. (iv) We deliver three practitioner artefacts ( Sec. 6 ): near-boundary selection, the SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) ( Brunton et al., 2016 ) δ OOD \delta_{\mathrm{OOD}} diagnostic, and a content/position-embedding (CE/PE) reframing verified architecture-invariant on Transformer ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) / Mamba ( Gu and Dao, 2023 ) / S4D ( Gu et al., 2022 ) ( 264 264 runs). (v) We map scope and limitations on a d d -torus benchmark, a periodic synthetic testbed ( Sec. 7 ): correct φ \varphi is necessary but not sufficient; model class and coverage continue to constrain OOD generalisation. Extended versions of tables are given in the appendix.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Multi-environment domain generalisation, formalised by IRM ( Arjovsky et al., 2019 ) and catalogued by Kaur et al. (2023) , breaks ties through invariance penalties across training distributions. Our single-window setting offers no such auxiliary environments, leaving OOD risk non-identifiable from data alone, and the commitment ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) supplies the structural information that multi-environment access supplies elsewhere. The Rashomon set ( Breiman, 2001 ; Xin et al., 2022 ) captures the same multiplicity at the model side: members agree on training data but disagree off-distribution, and ( φ , ψ ) (\varphi,\psi) acts as a canonicaliser that selects a Rashomon element whose extension matches the assumed DGP. A second body of work supplies the commitment implicitly via architecture or input format. PINNs ( Raissi et al., 2019 ) and Fourier Neural Operators ( Li et al., 2021 ) bake in a differential operator (constraint on ψ \psi ) or a Fourier basis (a φ \varphi that turns extrapolation into spectral interpolation), helping precisely when the assumed structure matches the DGP and degrading otherwise ( Sec. 7 ). Sinusoidal PE ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , RoPE ( Su et al., 2021 ) , and ALiBi ( Press et al., 2022 ) are partial periodic feature maps at the token-position level. Sec. 6.3 evaluates state-of-the-art architectures: Mamba ( Gu and Dao, 2023 ) and S4D ( Gu et al., 2022 ) . On the activation side, Ziyin et al. (2020) addresses the periodic-extrapolation failures by crafting an activation function with explicit periodic inductive bias, an ℳ \mathcal{M} -side commitment. In our controlled experiments, we show foundation models, TabPFN ( Hollmann et al., 2025 ) and TimesFM ( Das et al., 2024 ) , and how they inherit the same commitment problem through their input format: identical pretrained weights swing from chance to near-perfect when the user supplies a transformation ( Sec. 4.3 ), reframing input-format engineering as the practitioner-side delivery of the DGP commitment to a frozen model. Finally, we adopt SINDy ( Brunton et al., 2016 ) as a diagnostic: δ OOD \delta_{\mathrm{OOD}} , the OOD derivative residual after sparse fitting, correlates with the canonically-correct φ \varphi across our toy battery and four real-data experiments ( Sec. 6.2 ).

sections.heading: 4.3 Foundation models inherit DGP commitment via input format
sections.text: Pretrained foundation models do not escape the commitment; they inherit it via input format. On Exp. 1.1, TimesFM zero-shot reaches 8.9 % 8.9\% OOD on the sin ⁡ ( x ) \sin(x) context (vs. 155.9 % 155.9\% for raw- x x MLP) and drops to 1.0 % 1.0\% with a Fourier covariate; TabPFN goes from 226.2 % 226.2\% on raw x x to 0.1 % 0.1\% on Fourier columns. The mechanism is geometric: the Fourier map wraps train and OOD onto the same compact manifold S 1 S^{1} , so OOD becomes interpolation in feature space and TabPFN (a tabular regressor that does not extrapolate beyond the training input distribution) succeeds. The log \log map compresses but does not bound (Exp. 1.2: log ⁡ x train ∈ [ 0 , 0.69 ] \log x_{\mathrm{train}}\in[0,0.69] , log ⁡ x OOD ∈ [ 0.69 , 2.30 ] \log x_{\mathrm{OOD}}\in[0.69,2.30] ), so TabPFN with the correct ( log , log ) (\log,\log) map still clamps to the training y y -range and fails ( 85.4 % 85.4\% on P 1 P_{1} , comparable to its raw failure 80.3 % 80.3\% ); TimesFM with the matching covariate improves but lags ( 28.3 % 28.3\% on P 1 P_{1} , 29.6 % 29.6\% on P 2 P_{2} ). Linear OLS in the correct transformed space still wins by an order of magnitude. The right φ \varphi is necessary but not sufficient: the commitment requires a matching model class that extrapolates linearly in φ \varphi -space, which OLS and SINDy do by construction.

sections.heading: 5.3 Exp. 2.3: cross-species coding-DNA detection (biology)
sections.text: We classify 300 300 bp (base-pair) DNA reads as coding-DNA-sequence (CDS) vs. non-CDS. Genomes vary in GC content (% guanine–cytosine bases; the complement is AT, adenine–thymine); coding regions exhibit a 3-nucleotide codon period (H1), depletion of in-frame stop codons (H2), and a 21-class amino-acid (AA) composition (H3). We train on S. cerevisiae chromosomes I–IX and evaluate zero-shot on five organisms spanning 19 19 – 65 % 65\% GC ( Fig. 2 (c)). The shared base model is a ∼ 0.3 {\sim}0.3 M-parameter random-init Transformer encoder ( 2 2 layers, 4 4 heads, d = 128 d{=}128 ). We evaluate two non-FE heads (learned absolute positional encoding (APE), the DNABERT ( Ji et al., 2021 ) default; sinusoidal PE ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , denoted “sin”) and two FE heads (the codon-Fourier magnitude | FFT ⁡ ( h ) | ​ @ ​ P = 3 |\mathrm{FFT}(h)|@P{=}3 at the codon period (codon), capturing H1; and the biology head, which adds H2 in-frame stop counts and H3 amino-acid composition to the codon channel). The biologically inspired heads transfer at area under the ROC curve (AUROC) 0.718 0.718 – 0.960 0.960 zero-shot across the five OOD organisms. Panels: (a) representation alignment, (b) model-class capacity, (c) coverage, (d) noise robustness. Bands: ± 1 \pm 1 std over 100 seeds. When is the right representation not enough? We construct a periodic d d -torus benchmark in which the correct feature map is known exactly, then vary the model class ℳ \mathcal{M} , the sample budget, and noise levels ( Fig. 3 ). Three conditions emerge as jointly necessary: (a) representation alignment, (b) a model class expressing the residual interaction order q q of the target in 𝒵 x \mathcal{Z}_{x} , and (c) coverage N ≍ M crit d N\asymp M_{\mathrm{crit}}^{d} with M crit ≈ 4 M_{\mathrm{crit}}\approx 4 . The torus benchmark localises where the commitment runs out and the rest of the OOD problem (identifiability, capacity, sampling) takes over. Noise σ \sigma does not break the commitment (d). Critically, the canonical commitment retains a clear OOD advantage in both regimes ( ∼ 40 × \sim 40\times lower OOD error at low σ \sigma , ∼ 30 % {\sim}30\% smaller OOD error at high σ \sigma ): no in-window rule can detect this difference, only the choice of φ \varphi recovers it.

sections.heading: 8 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: Conclusion. OOD risk on a single training window is non-identifiable from data alone ( Proposition 1 ); the structural commitment ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) is the only information the modeller supplies that resolves it. A fixed architecture at identical ID loss can differ by ∼ 520 × {\sim}520\times OOD when only φ \varphi changes ( Tab. 1 ), and the mechanism transfers, untouched, to chemistry ( 0.0 % 0.0\% vs. 24.4 % 24.4\% OOD, Tab. 3 ), physics ( 2.1 % 2.1\% vs. 79.0 % 79.0\% , Tab. 4 ), biology (AUROC up to 0.96 0.96 vs. below-chance phase-equivariant readouts, Tab. 5 ), and Transformer/Mamba/S4D over 264 264 runs ( Sec. 6.3 ). This sharpens “feature engineering is dead”: deep learning supersedes hand-crafted features ID once samples and noise permit, but ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) remains the only ID-invisible signal that selects one extrapolation from the observationally-equivalent Rashomon class. Pretraining hides the commitment in the input format ( Sec. 4.3 ) without removing it; near-boundary loss and the SINDy δ OOD \delta_{\mathrm{OOD}} recover it as operational selection signals ( Sec. 6 ). Limitations. Proposition 1 ’s information-theoretic bound is tight only when ε ​ n ≪ σ \varepsilon\sqrt{n}\ll\sigma , our experiments sit in the signal-dominated regime where the bound is vacuous, though the multiplicity it characterises still binds CV in practice ( Sec. 6.1 ). Near-boundary validation requires accessible boundary samples, the SINDy diagnostic is silent on non-polynomial dynamics (e.g., G 2 = tanh ⁡ ( ⋅ ) G_{2}{=}\tanh(\cdot) ): δ OOD > 0 \delta_{\mathrm{OOD}}{>}0 flags “no sparse coordinate” but cannot rank. Correct φ \varphi is necessary, not sufficient: at N ≲ M crit d N\lesssim M_{\mathrm{crit}}^{d} ( M crit ≈ 4 M_{\mathrm{crit}}{\approx}4 ) or with a model class missing the residual interaction order q q , OOD collapses regardless ( Sec. 7 ). The CDS head fails on high-GC organisms (yeast-trained amino-acid weights mis-fire on M. tuberculosis ’s skewed codon usage). Future work. Two directions stand out: (i) a finite-sample OOD bound parametrised by sparse identifiability ( δ OOD \delta_{\mathrm{OOD}} of Sec. 6.2 ), extending Lemma 4 beyond exact realisability and (ii) robust automatic φ \varphi discovery with near boundary information connecting with multi-environment domain advancements.

sections.heading: Remark on the regime.
sections.text: The quantity ε ​ n / σ \varepsilon\sqrt{n}/\sigma is the effective signal-to-noise ratio after n n samples (signal scale ε \varepsilon , noise scale σ / n \sigma/\sqrt{n} ). The bound is informative when ε ​ n ≪ σ \varepsilon\sqrt{n}\ll\sigma (the noise-dominated regime, where the per-sample gap is drowned by noise; this is the proposition’s content and the regime characteristic of finite-window OOD problems) and vacuous (trivially ≤ 1 \leq 1 ) when ε ​ n ≫ σ \varepsilon\sqrt{n}\gg\sigma (the signal-dominated regime, where n n samples can reveal the gap). Selection criteria (cross-validation, training loss, held-out loss on W W ) are functions of the same W W -supported sample, hence special cases of a W W -supported test, and the bound applies to them by inclusion.

sections.heading: Provenance.
sections.text: The proof technique (Le Cam two-point + Pinsker) is classical [ Tsybakov, 2009 ] and the multiplicity it characterises is the Rashomon effect of Breiman [2001] , Xin et al. [2022] . Our contribution is the application to single-window OOD identifiability under the ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) commitment, not the inequality. The toy battery (Exp. 1.1, 1.2) and Exp. 3.1 sit in the signal-dominated regime where the bound is vacuous; the multiplicity it captures still binds in practice because the candidate hypothesis classes are observationally near-equivalent on W W , and ERM/CV select among them with the residual ambiguity that follows (Exp. 3.1, Sec. 6.1 ).

Feature Engineering as Identifiability Bias for OOD Generalization Leonel Aguilar Affiliation: Chair of Cognitive Science, ETH Zürich Email: aleonel@ethz.ch Jan Nagler Affiliation: Centre for Human and Machine Intelligence, Frankfurt School Email: j.nagler@fs.de Christoph Hoelscher Affiliation: Chair of Cognitive Science, ETH Zürich Email: choelsch@ethz.ch Nino Antulov-Fantulin Affiliation: Aisot Technologies AG, Affiliation: D-GESS, ETH Zürich Email: nino@aisot.ch Abstract Successful deep neural networks discover salient features of data. We show when and why they fail to learn out-of-distribution (OOD)-relevant representations from an in-distribution (ID) training window. This requires decoupling feature learning from data-generating-process (DGP) identifiability. From a single training window, OOD extrapolation is non-identifiable: infinitely many DGPs are ε \varepsilon -observationally equivalent on the training data but diverge arbitrarily outside it, and no in-distribution criterion alone reliably breaks the tie. A structural commitment, the feature map, label map, and model class ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) , dictates the assumed DGP and governs OOD generalization while leaving ID performance essentially unchanged. When architecture, pretraining, augmentation, input formats, or domain knowledge implicitly inject the missing commitment, the model succeeds. When it cannot infer OOD-relevant structure from ID evidence, it fails. Changing only the representation can make the same architecture, at the same in-distribution loss, differ by ∼ 520 × {\sim}520\times out of distribution. When the commitment is correct and identifiable, OOD error vanishes. For example, Fourier coordinates turn periodic extrapolation into interpolation on 𝕊 1 \mathbb{S}^{1} . The same mechanism predicts outcomes in three natural-science settings (mass-action chemistry; Kepler’s-third-law exoplanet prediction, n = 2,362 n=2{,}362 ; and cross-species coding-DNA detection) and in a 264-run positional-encoding study across Transformer, Mamba, and S4D. Finally, a controlled study shows: correct features are necessary but not sufficient. The model class must express the target, and the transformed training data must cover the relevant representation space. Thus, feature engineering is not a departure from what makes deep learning successful. It is the explicit structural commitment that makes extrapolation identifiable. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Left: sin ⁡ ( x ) \sin(x) (green) and its degree-9 Taylor polynomial (black) can be observationally equivalent (depending on noise and amount of samples) on the training window and diverge on [ π , 3 ​ π ] [\pi,3\pi] . Models (MLP, SINDy, TabPFN, TimesFM) trained/evaluated on the Original (raw) space without noise are shown. Right: in Fourier coordinates φ ⁡ ( x ) = ( sin ⁡ x , cos ⁡ x ) \varphi(x)=(\sin x,\cos x) , both (ID, OOD) map to the same circle 𝕊 1 \mathbb{S}^{1} , turning OOD extrapolation into interpolation. While the Universal Approximation Theorem guarantees that neural networks are exceptional interpolators within the support of their training data, they struggle with out-of-distribution extrapolation. Frameworks from Statistical Learning Theory provide guarantees for in-distribution generalization, however, achieving mathematically guaranteed extrapolation in deep learning remains an unsolved problem. We believe it is the right time to ask the question: When can neural networks extrapolate? We start our journey with a good old sin ⁡ ( x ) \sin(x) function. A neural network, 5 5 -hidden-layer MLP with 256 256 Tanh units, trained on raw f ⁡ ( x ) = sin ⁡ ( x ) f(x)=\sin(x) on [ − π , π ] [-\pi,\pi] ( Fig. 1 ) extrapolates as a smooth, eventually-levelling curve with high OOD relative error while an identical architecture trained on φ ⁡ ( x ) = ( sin ⁡ x , cos ⁡ x ) \varphi(x)=(\sin x,\cos x) reaches OOD relative error below 1 % 1\% ( Tab. 1 ). The two have indistinguishable training loss; they differ only in the feature map applied before the model. Two assumptions, periodic and polynomial-like (Taylor is a valid hypothesis on [ − π , π ] [-\pi,\pi] ), can be observationally equivalent on the training window and diverge outside it. The indistinguishability problem is structural. For any finite training window W W , infinitely many processes agree on W W to any fixed tolerance and disagree arbitrarily outside it. Proposition 1 formalises this as a worst-case lower bound on any in-distribution test, and cross-validation (CV) falls short empirically even outside that worst case ( Sec. 6.1 ). The modeller’s choice of representation space and model class breaks the tie. Correctness is relative to the model class. ( sin ⁡ x , cos ⁡ x ) (\sin x,\cos x) is the correct φ \varphi for sin ⁡ ( x ) \sin(x) only because the downstream class favours linear combinations: it renders the target linearly expressible. A Fourier-series regressor would collapse φ \varphi to the identity. Correctness is a joint property of ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) , which is why we treat them as a single commitment ( Sec. 3 ). Concrete failures of correct φ \varphi paired with non-matching ℳ \mathcal{M} appear in Sec. 4 . Three conditions are jointly necessary: (a) a representation ( φ , ψ ) (\varphi,\psi) aligned with the DGP, (b) a model class that expresses the target between 𝒵 x \mathcal{Z}_{x} and 𝒵 y \mathcal{Z}_{y} , and (c) coverage of 𝒵 x \mathcal{Z}_{x} sufficient to identify the model. (a)+(b) constitute the DGP commitment; (c) is its evidential prerequisite ( Sec. 7 ). The headline comparisons hold (b) and (c) fixed, isolating (a). Contributions: (i) We formalise observational equivalence on a finite window, identify ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) as the DGP commitment, prove ERM on W W is structurally blind to the choice, and characterise near-boundary data of width δ ≥ ε / r \delta\geq\varepsilon/r as the minimum heuristic that breaks the blindness ( Sec. 3 ). (ii) We isolate φ \varphi , ψ \psi , and ℳ \mathcal{M} in controlled experiments ( Sec. 4 ) on minimal pairs and on pretrained foundation models (TimesFM ( Das et al., 2024 ) , TabPFN ( Hollmann et al., 2025 ) , governed by the same mechanism via input format). (iii) We validate cross-domain ( Sec. 5 ) on chemistry (mass-action kinetics), physics (Kepler exoplanets, n = 2,362 n{=}2{,}362 ), and biology (cross-species coding-DNA-sequence (CDS) detection on six organisms), same prediction, all confirmed. (iv) We deliver three practitioner artefacts ( Sec. 6 ): near-boundary selection, the SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) ( Brunton et al., 2016 ) δ OOD \delta_{\mathrm{OOD}} diagnostic, and a content/position-embedding (CE/PE) reframing verified architecture-invariant on Transformer ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) / Mamba ( Gu and Dao, 2023 ) / S4D ( Gu et al., 2022 ) ( 264 264 runs). (v) We map scope and limitations on a d d -torus benchmark, a periodic synthetic testbed ( Sec. 7 ): correct φ \varphi is necessary but not sufficient; model class and coverage continue to constrain OOD generalisation. Extended versions of tables are given in the appendix. 2 Related Work Multi-environment domain generalisation, formalised by IRM ( Arjovsky et al., 2019 ) and catalogued by Kaur et al. (2023) , breaks ties through invariance penalties across training distributions. Our single-window setting offers no such auxiliary environments, leaving OOD risk non-identifiable from data alone, and the commitment ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) supplies the structural information that multi-environment access supplies elsewhere. The Rashomon set ( Breiman, 2001 ; Xin et al., 2022 ) captures the same multiplicity at the model side: members agree on training data but disagree off-distribution, and ( φ , ψ ) (\varphi,\psi) acts as a canonicaliser that selects a Rashomon element whose extension matches the assumed DGP. A second body of work supplies the commitment implicitly via architecture or input format. PINNs ( Raissi et al., 2019 ) and Fourier Neural Operators ( Li et al., 2021 ) bake in a differential operator (constraint on ψ \psi ) or a Fourier basis (a φ \varphi that turns extrapolation into spectral interpolation), helping precisely when the assumed structure matches the DGP and degrading otherwise ( Sec. 7 ). Sinusoidal PE ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , RoPE ( Su et al., 2021 ) , and ALiBi ( Press et al., 2022 ) are partial periodic feature maps at the token-position level. Sec. 6.3 evaluates state-of-the-art architectures: Mamba ( Gu and Dao, 2023 ) and S4D ( Gu et al., 2022 ) . On the activation side, Ziyin et al. (2020) addresses the periodic-extrapolation failures by crafting an activation function with explicit periodic inductive bias, an ℳ \mathcal{M} -side commitment. In our controlled experiments, we show foundation models, TabPFN ( Hollmann et al., 2025 ) and TimesFM ( Das et al., 2024 ) , and how they inherit the same commitment problem through their input format: identical pretrained weights swing from chance to near-perfect when the user supplies a transformation ( Sec. 4.3 ), reframing input-format engineering as the practitioner-side delivery of the DGP commitment to a frozen model. Finally, we adopt SINDy ( Brunton et al., 2016 ) as a diagnostic: δ OOD \delta_{\mathrm{OOD}} , the OOD derivative residual after sparse fitting, correlates with the canonically-correct φ \varphi across our toy battery and four real-data experiments ( Sec. 6.2 ). 3 Observational Equivalence and the DGP Commitment Setup. OOD risk on a single training window is non-identifiable from data alone ( Proposition 1 ); the structural commitment ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) is the only information the modeller supplies that resolves it. A fixed architecture at identical ID loss can differ by ∼ 520 × {\sim}520\times OOD when only φ \varphi changes ( Tab. 1 ), and the mechanism transfers, untouched, to chemistry ( 0.0 % 0.0\% vs. 24.4 % 24.4\% OOD, Tab. 3 ), physics ( 2.1 % 2.1\% vs. 79.0 % 79.0\% , Tab. 4 ), biology (AUROC up to 0.96 0.96 vs. below-chance phase-equivariant readouts, Tab. 5 ), and Transformer/Mamba/S4D over 264 264 runs ( Sec. 6.3 ). This sharpens “feature engineering is dead”: deep learning supersedes hand-crafted features ID once samples and noise permit, but ( φ , ψ , ℳ ) (\varphi,\psi,\mathcal{M}) remains the only ID-invisible signal that selects one extrapolation from the observationally-equivalent Rashomon class. Pretraining hides the commitment in the input format ( Sec. 4.3 ) without removing it; near-boundary loss and the SINDy δ OOD \delta_{\mathrm{OOD}} recover it as operational selection signals ( Sec. 6 ).
